quiz.question: What is the primary mathematical objective of the standard K-Means clustering algorithm?
options: To maximize the Margin between separating support vectors
To minimize the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS), also known as Inertia, between observations and their assigned cluster centroids
To maximize the cross-entropy loss between predicted and actual class labels
To find orthogonal eigenvectors that maximize total variance
quiz.explanation: K-Means seeks to minimize the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (Inertia): J = sum_j sum_{x in C_j} ||x - mu_j||^2. It iteratively assigns observations to the nearest centroid and recomputes centroids until convergence.

quiz.question: Why does K-Means++ initialization provide substantially superior convergence guarantees compared to standard random centroid initialization?
options: It initializes centroids using gradient descent on GPUs

It samples the first centroid uniformly at random and then selects subsequent centroids with probability proportional to the squared distance D(x)^2 from the nearest existing centroid, ensuring well-dispersed starting points
It runs DBSCAN first to find the cluster density peaks
It automatically identifies the optimal number of clusters K without an elbow plot
quiz.explanation: K-Means++ selects initial centers with probability P(x) = D(x)^2 / sum(D(x')^2). Points far from already chosen centers are much more likely to be selected, avoiding clustered initial centers and reducing poor local minima.

quiz.question: Why is minimizing Inertia alone insufficient for determining the optimal number of clusters K in K-Means?
options: Because Inertia is only defined for 1-dimensional datasets
Because Inertia monotonically decreases as K increases, reaching exactly 0 when K equals the number of samples N (each point is its own centroid)
Because Inertia can only be computed when true target labels are known
Because Scikit-learn does not expose an inertia_ attribute
quiz.explanation: Adding more centroids always reduces within-cluster distances. When K=N, Inertia=0. Therefore, practitioners use the Elbow Method (point of diminishing returns) and Silhouette Score to balance compactness with model simplicity.

quiz.question: In Silhouette Analysis, what does an individual observation score of s(i) = -0.3 indicate?
options: The observation is located at the exact center of its assigned cluster
The observation is, on average, closer to points in a neighboring cluster than to points in its own assigned cluster, indicating likely misclustering
The observation has zero Euclidean distance to all other points
The dataset has zero variance along the first principal component
quiz.explanation: The Silhouette coefficient is s(i) = (b(i) - a(i)) / max(a(i), b(i)). When a(i) > b(i), s(i) becomes negative, meaning the sample is on average closer to a neighboring cluster than to members of its own cluster.

quiz.question: What is the key operational distinction between Single Linkage and Complete Linkage in Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering?
options: Single linkage uses Manhattan distance; Complete linkage uses Cosine similarity
Single linkage measures the minimum pairwise distance between clusters (prone to chaining); Complete linkage measures the maximum pairwise distance (producing compact, spherical clusters)
Single linkage is top-down; Complete linkage is bottom-up
Single linkage requires Gaussian distributions
quiz.explanation: Single Linkage defines cluster distance as D(A, B) = min d(a, b), which can link disparate clusters via thin chains of nearby points. Complete Linkage defines distance as D(A, B) = max d(a, b), enforcing compact cluster diameters.

quiz.question: How does DBSCAN define a 'Core Point' in a dataset?
options: A point that has the highest silhouette coefficient in the dataset
A point whose epsilon (eps) neighborhood contains at least min_samples observations (including itself)
A point located at the geometric center of all observations
A point that has zero distance to an existing centroid
quiz.explanation: In DBSCAN, a point is a core point if |N_eps(x)| >= min_samples. Core points form dense cluster interiors from which density-reachable border points are expanded. Isolated points become noise (-1).

quiz.question: Why is DBSCAN fundamentally superior to K-Means when clustering datasets with complex non-convex geometries (e.g. concentric circles or interleaving moons)?
options: DBSCAN uses linear regression lines to bisect the data
DBSCAN discovers clusters based on contiguous high-density connectivity rather than distance to spherical centroids, allowing it to trace arbitrary non-linear shapes while filtering noise
DBSCAN projects data onto 100 dimensions automatically
DBSCAN guarantees equal cluster sizes
quiz.explanation: K-Means relies on Voronoi cells around centroids, forcing convex/spherical cluster partitions. DBSCAN connects points via continuous density paths, effortlessly tracing moons, rings, and arbitrary non-linear shapes.

quiz.question: What is the core advantage of Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) with Expectation-Maximization over K-Means?
options: GMM requires zero hyperparameter choices
GMM provides soft (probabilistic) cluster assignments and accommodates non-spherical ellipsoidal cluster shapes through component covariance matrices (full, tied, diag, spherical)
GMM runs 10x faster than K-Means on large datasets
GMM completely eliminates the need for feature scaling
quiz.explanation: While K-Means performs hard assignment to spherical clusters, GMM calculates posterior responsibilities gamma_ik = P(z_i = k | x_i) (soft clustering) and fits parameterized covariance matrices to represent elliptical, oriented distributions.

quiz.question: How do AIC (Akaike Information Criterion) and BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) assist in selecting the number of components K in a Gaussian Mixture Model?
options: They measure the training speed in milliseconds
They balance model goodness-of-fit (log-likelihood) against model parameter complexity (degrees of freedom), penalizing over-parameterized models so the minimum value identifies the optimal K
They enforce that all Gaussian components have identical variance
They calculate the Adjusted Rand Index against test labels
quiz.explanation: AIC = 2p - 2ln(L) and BIC = p*ln(N) - 2ln(L). As components increase, likelihood improves but parameter count p grows. The minimum of the AIC/BIC curve identifies the model that best explains the data with minimal over-parameterization.

quiz.question: What is the RFM framework commonly used in enterprise customer segmentation clustering projects?
options: Random Forest Modeling (Recalculate, Fit, Measure)
Recency (how recently did the customer purchase), Frequency (how often do they purchase), and Monetary Value (total spend)
Residual Feature Minimization
Robust Feature Matching
quiz.explanation: RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary Value) is the premier behavioral framework for customer segmentation. Engineering RFM features followed by scaling and clustering (e.g. K-Means or GMM) discovers actionable segments like VIPs, at-risk churners, and budget shoppers.
